title: THE BOOK OF THE BIBLE THAT MAKES CHRISTIANS BLUSH: DID GOD REALLY PUT SEXUAL DESIRE IN HOLY SCRIPTURE?
paragraphs: THE BOOK OF THE BIBLE THAT MAKES CHRISTIANS BLUSH: DID GOD REALLY PUT SEXUAL DESIRE IN HOLY SCRIPTURE?

Why Song of Songs makes some believers uncomfortable, what its ancient Hebrew actually reveals, and how a book filled with kisses, longing, beauty, and intimacy exposes something much deeper about shame, holiness, marriage, and the God who refuses to abandon broken people.
There is a book in your Bible that some Christians would rather you never read aloud in church.
Not because it teaches heresy.
Not because it promotes rebellion.
Not because it contradicts the holiness of God.
But because it talks about something many believers have spent their entire lives being taught to fear, suppress, or feel ashamed of.
Desire.
Not merely the desire to worship. Not simply the longing for heaven.
The desire to be kissed. To be held. To be wanted. To experience the tenderness and physical intimacy of romantic love.
And here is where things become uncomfortable.
God allowed those words to become part of Holy Scripture.
Not hidden in an obscure manuscript. Not buried in some forbidden religious text.
Right there in the Bible you carry to church.
The same Bible that commands purity contains a woman saying:
“Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth: for thy love is better than wine.” — Song of Solomon 1:2, KJV
Read that again.
She is not apologizing for wanting affection.
She is not describing herself as spiritually defective because she longs for someone.
She is speaking openly, poetically, passionately.
And the inspired book does not interrupt her with a condemnation.
So why do so many Christians become uncomfortable when they encounter the Song of Songs?
Why do some pastors rarely preach from it?
Why have generations of believers sometimes treated this biblical love poetry as though its literal meaning were too embarrassing to acknowledge?
And perhaps the most important question of all:
If God created human desire, when did we begin treating every expression of desire as though it were dirty?
Before we answer, we need to confront something that could change how you understand your own body, your marriage, your wounds, your temptations, and the grace of Jesus Christ.
Because the Song of Songs does not teach that every desire should be obeyed.
But neither does it teach that every desire should be despised.
And somewhere between those two truths, many Christians have been living in unnecessary shame.
The Hebrew title of this extraordinary biblical book is שִׁיר הַשִּׁירִים — Shir haShirim.
Literally, “Song of Songs.”
In Hebrew, this construction can express excellence or supremacy, much like “Holy of Holies” or “King of Kings.”
It is a way of saying that this is a song of extraordinary distinction.
The opening verse reads:
שִׁיר הַשִּׁירִים אֲשֶׁר לִשְׁלֹמֹה
Shir haShirim asher liShlomoh.
“The song of songs, which is Solomon's.” — Song of Solomon 1:1, KJV

The Hebrew phrase asher liShlomoh associates the book with Solomon, although scholars debate whether it identifies Solomon as its author, its subject, its dedicatee, or the figure with whom the song is traditionally associated.
That distinction matters.
We should not claim certainty where Scripture's wording leaves room for discussion.
But something else is unmistakable.
This book is poetry.
Ancient Hebrew love poetry.
Its language is filled with fragrance, vineyards, gardens, flowers, fruit, embraces, longing, and the beauty of the beloved.
It is not written like the commandments in Exodus.
It is not written like Paul's letters to the churches.
It is not written like a historical account of Israel's kings.
It is an artistic celebration of love, expressed through vivid images that ancient hearers would have understood differently from how modern readers sometimes understand them.
And yes, physical attraction is genuinely part of its subject.
The lovers admire one another's bodies.
They express longing for closeness.
They delight in being desired.
They speak of love with a boldness that can surprise readers accustomed to hearing the Bible discussed only in terms of rules, judgment, and religious obligation.
Consider Song of Solomon 7:10:
“I am my beloved's, and his desire is toward me.” — KJV
The Hebrew says:
אֲנִי לְדוֹדִי וְעָלַי תְּשׁוּקָתוֹ
Ani ledodi, ve'alai teshuqato.
“I am my beloved's, and his desire is toward me.”
The word תְּשׁוּקָה — teshuqah — refers to desire or longing.
It is also found in Genesis 3:16 and Genesis 4:7, although the meaning and circumstances of those passages differ.
Here, in Song of Songs, desire is not presented as something inherently shameful.
The woman recognizes that she is loved and desired.
And she speaks with confidence.
There is tenderness in that.
There is dignity.
There is mutuality.
And there is something profoundly important for a culture that has often taught people to measure their worth by whether someone finds them attractive.
The woman in this poem is not merely an object being admired.
She has a voice.
She expresses her own affection.
She describes her own longing.
She participates in the relationship rather than existing merely as the passive recipient of someone else's desire.
That does not mean the poem answers every modern question about marriage, gender, sexuality, or relationships.
It does not.
But it does reveal something we should never ignore.
The Bible is not embarrassed by the goodness of embodied human love.
And neither should we be.
Yet here is where we must be careful.
Because the world often takes a truth that God created and stretches it until it becomes a lie.
God created food.
But gluttony is not therefore holy.
God created the human capacity for anger.
But destructive rage is not therefore righteous.
God created human sexuality.
But that does not mean every sexual desire, fantasy, relationship, or action receives His approval.
Creation establishes that something can be good.
It does not establish that every possible use of that thing is good.
This is where Christian teaching must recover both courage and clarity.
We do not need to condemn the body to defend holiness.
And we do not need to abandon holiness to celebrate the body.
Genesis tells us that God created humanity male and female and declared His creation very good (Genesis 1:27, 31).
Genesis 2:24 describes the marriage union in which a man and woman become one flesh.
Genesis 2:25 then records something remarkable:
“And they were both naked, the man and his wife, and were not ashamed.” — KJV
Not ashamed.
Before sin entered the human story, nakedness within that original marriage was not presented as a source of disgrace.
There was no hiding.
No exploitation.
No manipulation.
No betrayal.
No fear of being seen.
But after humanity's disobedience, the story changes.
Adam and Eve recognize their nakedness, cover themselves, and hide from God.
Genesis 3:10 records Adam saying:
“I was afraid, because I was naked; and I hid myself.” — KJV
Notice the movement.
From openness to hiding.
From innocence to fear.
From trust to alienation.
Sin did not merely introduce forbidden actions into human experience.
It fractured relationships—with God, with one another, and even with our understanding of ourselves.
And that fracture still echoes today.
Some people have been taught that their bodies are inherently disgusting.
Others have been taught that their bodies exist primarily to satisfy someone else's appetite.
Some carry shame because of sexual sin they willingly committed.
Others carry shame because of abuse, coercion, or betrayal that was committed against them.
Those are not the same experiences.
And they must never be treated as though they are.
If someone violated you, the responsibility for that violation belongs to the person who committed it.
You do not need to repent for being harmed.
You deserve protection, care, and the opportunity to heal.
And if you have sinned sexually, Scripture does not require you to pretend it never happened.
It calls you to repentance and offers forgiveness through Jesus Christ.
Both truths matter.
Because grace does not erase moral responsibility.
And holiness does not justify cruelty toward wounded people.
Now return to the Song of Songs.
Listen to the woman in Song of Solomon 2:16:
“My beloved is mine, and I am his: he feedeth among the lilies.” — KJV
There is a beautiful reciprocity in those words.
My beloved is mine.
And I am his.
Not ownership in the sense of treating another human being as property.
But the poetic language of mutual belonging and devotion.
Love is not simply the satisfaction of an appetite.
It involves giving and receiving.
Trusting and being trustworthy.
Being known and choosing to know another person faithfully.
This is one reason reducing Song of Songs to a book about sexual pleasure alone would be a serious mistake.
Sexual desire is present.
But it is not the entire story.
The poem also portrays admiration, affection, longing, exclusivity, delight, vulnerability, and the astonishing power of love.
And then we encounter one of its most unforgettable passages.

“Set me as a seal upon thine heart, as a seal upon thine arm: for love is strong as death; jealousy is cruel as the grave: the coals thereof are coals of fire, which hath a most vehement flame.” — Song of Solomon 8:6, KJV
The Hebrew expression near the end is:
שַׁלְהֶבֶתְיָה
Shalhevetyah.

It is commonly understood as an intense or mighty flame. Some interpreters understand its final element, Yah, as a reference to the divine name, giving the sense of “a flame of Yah,” while others understand the construction as expressing extraordinary intensity.
This is one of those places where translation and interpretation require humility.
We should not build an entire doctrine on a disputed Hebrew expression.
But the force of the passage is clear.
Love is powerful.
It burns.
It demands seriousness.
It cannot be reduced to a passing emotional thrill.
The following verse declares:
“Many waters cannot quench love, neither can the floods drown it.” — Song of Solomon 8:7, KJV
Think about that.
A love that cannot simply be purchased.
A love that refuses to be measured by material wealth.
A love whose power is compared to fire and whose endurance is pictured against overwhelming waters.
Does that sound like the Bible celebrating careless indulgence?
No.
It sounds like the Bible taking love far more seriously than a culture that often treats people as disposable.
And perhaps that is why this book makes some of us uncomfortable.
Not only because it speaks about physical desire.
But because it refuses to separate desire from the deeper question of what love actually is.
It forces us to ask whether we have confused attention with affection.
Whether we have confused lust with intimacy.
Whether we have confused being wanted with being cherished.
Whether we have confused the excitement of being pursued with the security of being faithfully loved.
And some of us know exactly how painful those confusions can become.
You thought that person loved you.
You trusted the promises.
You believed the late-night conversations.
You believed that intimacy meant commitment.
You gave someone access to places in your heart you had protected for years.
Then something changed.
The messages became shorter.
The affection became conditional.
The promises disappeared.
And suddenly you were left wondering whether you had ever truly been loved at all.
Maybe your story is different.
Maybe you are married, but the tenderness has faded.
You share a home.
You share responsibilities.
You share bills, schedules, and the exhausting routines of ordinary life.
But somewhere along the way, you stopped feeling seen.
You can sit beside someone and still feel terribly alone.
Or perhaps you are single, faithfully trying to honor Christ, yet secretly wondering whether longing for marriage, affection, or physical closeness means your spiritual life is weak.
It does not.
Desire itself is not proof that you are far from God.
But desire must be brought under the wisdom and lordship of God.
And sometimes the holiest response to a longing is not immediate fulfillment.
Sometimes it is patience.
Sometimes it is restraint.
Sometimes it is leaving a relationship that continually pulls you away from Christ.
Sometimes it is confessing sin.
Sometimes it is learning that loneliness does not make you less valuable.
And sometimes it is discovering that no human being, however loving, can carry the full weight of your need for salvation, identity, and ultimate security.
Only Jesus Christ can do that.
This brings us to a question Christians have debated for centuries.
If Song of Songs celebrates human romantic love, why have so many believers interpreted it as a picture of God's love for His people?
The answer deserves more than a dismissive sentence.
Jewish interpreters have long read the Song in relation to God's covenant love for Israel.
Christian interpreters, including influential figures in the early church and medieval tradition, have often read it in relation to Christ and His Church, or to the soul's longing for God.
Those traditions were not necessarily attempts to pretend the book contains no romantic language.
Many interpreters believed that its imagery could communicate spiritual realities beyond the immediate human relationship portrayed in the poetry.
And Scripture itself gives us reasons to understand marriage as capable of pointing beyond itself.
In Ephesians 5:31–32, Paul quotes Genesis concerning the union of husband and wife and then writes:
Paul explicitly uses marriage as an image through which to speak about Christ and His people.
That is biblical.
But there is an important distinction.
Ephesians explicitly makes that connection. Song of Songs does not explicitly identify its lovers as Jesus and the Church.
We must not pretend that every reference to a garden, breast, kiss, or embrace is a secret code that must be decoded into a specific spiritual doctrine.
Doing so can obscure the actual beauty of the biblical poem.
A responsible Christian reading can acknowledge the Song's literal celebration of human love while also reflecting on how faithful covenant love may point toward the greater love revealed in Christ.
These readings need not be enemies.
But the spiritual application should not erase the poem's human meaning.
Nor should we force Jesus into every metaphor as though the Bible were incapable of speaking positively about marriage.
And this brings us to another uncomfortable truth.
Some Christians avoid Song of Songs because they have inherited an attitude toward sexuality that is more fearful than biblical.
Others avoid it because the book is difficult to teach wisely in mixed-age congregations.
Some worry that its imagery will be misunderstood.
Some are uncertain how to reconcile its passionate poetry with biblical sexual ethics.
And others simply have not studied its literary form closely enough to feel confident preaching it.
These reasons are not all equally justified.
Nor is every pastor who rarely preaches Song of Songs secretly ashamed of sexuality.
We should resist making accusations about people's motives.
But we should also recognize that avoiding difficult passages indefinitely can leave believers poorly equipped to understand them.
When the church refuses to speak thoughtfully about desire, people do not stop experiencing desire.
They often begin learning about it somewhere else.
And the loudest voices outside the church are not always interested in teaching love, faithfulness, self-control, or human dignity.
That should concern us.
Because the answer to a distorted view of sexuality is not silence.
It is truth.
And truth must be taught with both conviction and compassion.
Song of Solomon 2:7 contains a repeated warning:
“I charge you, O ye daughters of Jerusalem, by the roes, and by the hinds of the field, that ye stir not up, nor awake my love, till he please.” — KJV
The Hebrew includes the expression:
עַד שֶׁתֶּחְפָּץ
Ad shetechpatz.
Often rendered along the lines of “until it pleases” or “until it desires.”
The precise nuance of the refrain is debated, but its repeated appearance emphasizes that love has its own appropriate timing and should not be carelessly stirred or forced.
This is not a complete sexual ethics manual.
But it is a meaningful reminder that desire is not something to manipulate recklessly.
And when we read this alongside the broader teaching of Scripture, we encounter a consistent call to honor God with our bodies.
Paul writes:
And in 1 Corinthians 6:19–20, he reminds believers that their bodies belong to God and that they are to glorify Him in their bodies.
Biblical Christianity does not say the body is worthless.
It says the body matters so much that what we do with it has moral and spiritual significance.
Sexual holiness is not hatred of physical intimacy.
It is the recognition that physical intimacy is too meaningful to be treated carelessly.
Within the Bible's teaching on marriage, sexual union is not presented as something shameful.
Hebrews 13:4 says:
“Marriage is honourable in all, and the bed undefiled: but whoremongers and adulterers God will judge.” — KJV
Notice how the verse holds two truths together.
Marriage is honorable.
Sexual immorality is not.
The Bible does not require us to choose between celebrating God's good gifts and respecting His moral boundaries.
It commands us to do both.
But now I want to speak to the person who has been reading all of this with a quiet ache in the chest.
The person whose story does not resemble a beautiful love poem.
You may have crossed boundaries you once promised yourself you would never cross.
You may have remained in a relationship because you were afraid no one else would love you.
You may have used sexual attention to quiet a loneliness that returned the moment you were alone.
You may have been unfaithful.
You may be fighting pornography, lust, secrecy, or habits that have begun to control you.
Or you may simply be carrying the grief of a marriage that has not become what you prayed it would be.
And perhaps the hardest part is not what other people know.
It is what you know.
The memories.
The compromises.
The things you cannot undo.
The moments you wish you could erase.
The person you were before everything became complicated.
Listen carefully.
Your past is real. But it does not have to be the final authority over your future.
That is not because sin is insignificant.
It is because Jesus Christ is a greater Savior than we could ever deserve.
Consider the woman in John 8.
She was brought before Jesus after being caught in adultery.
Her accusers wanted judgment.
They used her disgrace as a weapon.
Jesus did not declare adultery acceptable.
But neither did He join the crowd in destroying her.
After her accusers departed, He told her:
“Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more.” — John 8:11, KJV
Grace.
And repentance.
Mercy.
And transformation.
Not grace without truth.
Not truth without mercy.
Both, spoken by the Savior.

The passage is traditionally included in John 7:53–8:11, although it is absent from some of the earliest surviving manuscripts of John's Gospel. That textual history deserves acknowledgment rather than concealment. The mercy and moral seriousness displayed in the account are also consistent with teachings clearly established elsewhere in the New Testament.
Romans 8:1 declares:
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus.” — KJV
And 1 John 1:9 promises:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” — KJV
That is the Gospel.
Not pretending your choices never mattered.
Not calling darkness light.
Not trying to purchase forgiveness through religious activity.
But coming honestly to the crucified and risen Christ, trusting His mercy, turning from sin, and learning to walk in newness of life.
And if your wounds came from another person's wrongdoing, His compassion is not withheld from you because of what someone else did.
He sees the wounded as well as the guilty.
He is not confused about the difference.
The cross reveals the seriousness of sin.
The resurrection reveals that sin and death do not have the final word over those who belong to Christ.
And that is why the message of grace is so much greater than an invitation to feel better about ourselves.
It is an invitation to be reconciled to God.
To be forgiven.
To be made new.
To have our desires reordered by His Spirit.
To learn a love that is not ruled by selfishness.
A love that does not use people.
A love that tells the truth.
A love that knows how to repent.
A love that refuses to call exploitation intimacy.
A love that learns faithfulness even when faithfulness is difficult.
A love shaped by Jesus.
And here is the beautiful connection.
Song of Songs celebrates the wonder of human love.
But the Gospel reveals the Savior who makes redeemed human life possible.
The poem can teach us to appreciate the beauty of faithful affection.
Jesus teaches us the greater reality of self-giving love.
The poem speaks of longing.
Jesus meets our deepest need for reconciliation with God.
The poem describes a love as strong as death.
Jesus actually entered death and rose victorious.
These are theological reflections across Scripture, not claims that every line of Song of Songs secretly predicts the crucifixion.
And that distinction makes the beauty more meaningful, not less.
Because we do not have to distort one biblical book to honor another.
All Scripture belongs within God's unfolding revelation, and all Scripture should be read faithfully in its own context.
So was Song of Songs written to celebrate sexual desire?
Yes, in a meaningful but carefully qualified sense.
It celebrates romantic attraction, embodied affection, longing, and the delight of lovers in one another.
But it does not celebrate desire detached from love, wisdom, commitment, and moral responsibility.
It is more than a celebration of sexual appetite.
It is a poetic testimony to the beauty and power of human love.
And Christians do not need to be embarrassed by that.
We need to understand it.
We need to teach it responsibly.
We need to stop confusing shame with holiness.
And we need to stop confusing unrestricted desire with freedom.
Because neither extreme reflects the fullness of biblical truth.
Perhaps you came into this article expecting an argument about a controversial book.
But somewhere along the way, the question became personal.
What have you been taught about love?
What have you believed about your body?
What wounds are you still carrying?
What desires have you allowed to rule you?
What shame have you mistaken for the voice of God?
What sin have you been defending because repentance feels frightening?
And what would change if you stopped hiding from the One who already knows the truth?
Jesus does not invite you to come because your history is spotless.
He calls sinners to repentance.
He calls the weary to Himself.
He offers mercy that we could never earn.
And He does not leave those who follow Him unchanged.
Maybe today your prayer does not need to be elaborate.
Maybe it is simply this:

“Lord Jesus, teach me to love what You love. Forgive what I have done wrong. Heal what has been wounded. Purify my desires. Teach me to honor You with my body, my relationships, my choices, and my heart. I do not want to keep hiding. I want to walk in Your truth. Amen.”
If that prayer describes something happening inside you, I would love to hear from you.
You do not have to disclose private details to strangers to be sincere before God.
But sometimes a simple, honest word becomes the beginning of an encouraging conversation between believers who realize they are not walking alone.
Return to the Scriptures.

Read Song of Songs slowly, preferably in a translation you understand, and consider its poetry alongside Genesis, the teachings of Jesus, and the New Testament's instruction about marriage and holiness.
Do not settle for an isolated verse.
Seek the whole counsel of God.
Someone in your family may be silently struggling with shame.
A married couple may need to rediscover the biblical dignity of tenderness and faithfulness.
A young believer may need to hear that sexual desire is not automatically a reason to despise themselves.
Someone caught in sin may need both a loving warning and the hope of forgiveness.
Someone who does not yet know Jesus may discover that Christianity is not merely a collection of prohibitions, but the announcement of a Savior who forgives sinners and restores broken lives.
Sometimes sharing truth is an act of love.
And sometimes love means protecting another person's dignity rather than putting their struggle on public display.
We want to keep pointing people beyond religious appearances and toward the living Christ.
Beyond shallow motivation and toward biblical discipleship.
Beyond temporary emotional excitement and toward enduring spiritual growth.
And if this ministry has helped you, I want to extend a personal invitation.
It is not a requirement for salvation.
It does not make you more righteous than someone who cannot afford to give.
And it should never replace the responsibilities you have to your family, your local church, or those in genuine need.
But it can be a meaningful, voluntary expression of generosity and partnership in Gospel ministry.
And 2 Corinthians 9:7 reminds us that giving should not come from compulsion:
“God loveth a cheerful giver.” — KJV
And it can help sustain the work of making discipleship resources accessible.
The greater invitation is to participate in a continuing work of biblical encouragement, discipleship, and Gospel-centered storytelling.
Read.
Learn.
Pray.
Make use of the free resources.
Your worth in Christ is not determined by your ability to contribute financially.
A person who shares a message with someone who desperately needs it may be participating in something far more significant than they realize.
Because the goal has never been simply to build a large audience.
The goal is to point people to Jesus.
To encourage repentance without crushing the repentant.
To proclaim grace without minimizing sin.
To teach holiness without producing needless shame.
To remind broken people that redemption is possible through the Savior who died and rose again.
And perhaps that is the final lesson we should carry away from the Song of Songs.
God did not create us to live as though love were something filthy.
Nor did He create us to worship our desires.
He calls us to receive His gifts with gratitude, honor His boundaries with obedience, and recognize that even the most beautiful earthly love cannot replace the Lord who made us.
The Song celebrates love.
The Gospel reveals the Redeemer.
And when the Redeemer takes hold of a human life, even the chapters we wish we could tear out do not have to be the chapters that define us forever.
The pages you are ashamed to remember may become the very place where you discover how deeply you need the Savior who refuses to stop writing your story.
